blocks.text: The earlier lesson compared MCP to hand rolled, in house tool calling code. This one compares it to something different, an actual product feature, proprietary plugin systems like the early ChatGPT plugins.

Both traditional tool calling and early plugin systems solved a real problem, letting a model reach outside itself. But plugins added a public marketplace and a specific vendor format on top, and that is exactly where the comparison to MCP gets interesting.
This lesson walks through why a plugin built for one AI product simply does not run anywhere else, and why MCP has spread across vendors in a way earlier plugin efforts never quite managed.
By the end, you should be able to explain this tradeoff clearly in an interview setting.
1. What Early Plugin Systems Actually Were

blocks.alt: Plugins reach only inside one product while MCP reaches across many

blocks.text: Around 2023, ChatGPT shipped a plugin system, developers described an API using a manifest file and an OpenAPI schema, and ChatGPT could call it during a conversation.

It was a real and useful idea, letting a model book a flight or query a private knowledge base felt new at the time. The catch was the format, the hosting rules, and the review process all belonged to one company.
Other AI products soon shipped their own separate plugin or extension formats, each with its own manifest shape and review process.
Real Products That Shipped Plugins

items: Travel and shopping companies wrote a ChatGPT plugin so users could book or browse from inside a chat.
Internal company tools sometimes got a plugin wrapper so employees could query them through ChatGPT.
Each of these plugins lived in ChatGPT's plugin store and nowhere else.
None of them could be pointed at a different AI product without a separate build.

blocks.text: That last point is the whole story in one sentence, and the rest of this lesson just unpacks why it matters.
2. The Manifest File, Tied to One Product
A ChatGPT plugin needed a specific file, ai plugin dot json, placed at a specific path, describing the plugin in a format only ChatGPT understood.
Notice the shape here is bound to one host's expectations, the field names, the required auth block, even the hosting path are all decisions made by that one vendor.
Even the auth block only supports the handful of authentication styles that one vendor decided to support, another vendor's host might expect something else entirely.
3. The Same Idea, Written as an MCP Server
Now compare that to the same weather lookup exposed as an MCP server. Nothing here mentions any particular chat product at all.
This server speaks a generic protocol over standard input and output or over HTTP, not a format invented by one company for its own product.
The transport choice, stdio for a local server or HTTP for a remote one, is also part of the open spec, so any client knows how to connect either way.
4. Why a Plugin Cannot Just Move to Another Product

blocks.alt: A plugin tied to one product is compared against an MCP server that works elsewhere

blocks.text: Suppose a team wants their ChatGPT weather plugin to also work inside a different assistant. The manifest format is not understood there, the auth block means something different, and the whole review and discovery flow does not exist on the other side.

The team's only real option is rewriting the integration a second time, from scratch, targeting that other product's own proprietary format. The underlying fetch_weather logic barely changes, but the wrapper around it has to be rebuilt entirely.
5. Why an MCP Server Simply Works Elsewhere

The get_weather server from section 3 needs no rewrite to be used by a second host. Any MCP compatible client, whatever it is built by, speaks the same tools slash list and tools slash call messages covered in the earlier MCP Workflow lesson.
Point a second host's MCP client configuration at the same server process, and it is done, no new manifest, no second review, no vendor specific auth block to satisfy.
Discovery, Store Submission Versus a Live Call
Getting a ChatGPT plugin in front of users meant submitting it to a plugin store and waiting on a review process controlled by one company.
An MCP server needs no store and no review board, a client simply calls tools slash list at connection time and sees whatever the server currently offers.
6. Vendor Lock In, By Design Versus By Accident

blocks.alt: Lock in by design is compared against lock in by accident

blocks.text: It is worth being fair here, ChatGPT plugins were not built to lock developers in out of malice, the format simply had to be something, and that something happened to belong to one company.
MCP's open specification exists specifically to avoid that outcome, no single company owns the format, and any vendor can implement a client or a server against the same public spec.
A Concrete Example of That Risk
ChatGPT's original plugin store was eventually phased out in favor of a different feature, and plugins built against it stopped being reachable the way they once were.
Anyone who had invested only in that one proprietary format felt that shift directly, an MCP server built the same year keeps working regardless of any single host's roadmap changes.
7. Who Governs the Format
A proprietary plugin format changes whenever the owning company decides to change it, sometimes with little notice to developers who built against the old version.
MCP's specification is published openly, versioned, and shaped by input from multiple companies building clients and servers against it, not by one vendor's internal roadmap alone.
Anyone can read the spec, propose a change, or point out a gap, which is simply not possible with a format one company keeps entirely to itself.
8. The Tradeoff, More Work Upfront

blocks.alt: More work upfront is compared against more reach later

blocks.text: Building against an open standard is rarely the fastest path on day one. A quick, vendor specific plugin can sometimes be shipped in an afternoon by following that one product's own quirky rules closely.
An MCP server asks for a little more discipline upfront, a proper schema, a real transport choice, following a spec that was not written with any single team's shortcuts in mind.

items: Writing a proper input schema for each tool, not just whatever fields one product happened to require.
Picking a transport, stdio for local use or HTTP for a remote server, and testing it works.
Running the server against a real MCP client during development, instead of one product's specific test console.

blocks.text: 9. The Tradeoff, More Reach Later
That upfront cost buys something real, the same server keeps working as new MCP compatible hosts show up, with no extra rewrite required for each one.
A vendor specific plugin never gets that benefit for free, every new product it needs to reach is another rewrite, another review, another format to learn.

blocks.text: 11. Why Adoption Spread Further for MCP

blocks.alt: One MCP server reaches many host applications at once

blocks.text: Early plugin systems asked every other AI vendor to adopt one company's specific format, which is a hard sell, no competitor wants to build against a rival's proprietary rules.

MCP instead asked vendors to adopt a neutral, shared specification that nobody owns outright, so competing companies could all implement clients and servers against it without favoring any single vendor.
12. Network Effects Working in MCP's Favor

blocks.alt: More servers attract more hosts, which attracts even more servers

blocks.text: Every new MCP server built by any team adds value to every existing MCP client, and every new client adds an audience to every existing server. That loop grows on its own.

blocks.title: Why this compounds
blocks.content: A plugin marketplace grows the reach of exactly one product. An open protocol's ecosystem grows the reach of every client and every server built against it, at the same time.

blocks.text: This is the same dynamic that made open web standards outcompete closed alternatives over the long run.
13. What This Does Not Mean
None of this means proprietary plugin systems were a bad idea at the time, they solved a real problem before an open alternative existed.
It also does not mean every open standard automatically wins, MCP earned its adoption by being genuinely simple to implement, not just by being open on paper.
A complicated open standard that nobody wants to implement gets the same fate as a closed one, low adoption.
14. Worked Example, Shipping the Same Tool Both Ways
A small team builds an internal document search tool. Shipped as a ChatGPT plugin, it works well for the handful of staff using ChatGPT, and that is the entire audience it will ever reach.

Six months later, half the team moves to a different assistant that supports MCP. The document search tool, if it had been an MCP server from the start, would already work there, no second build required.
The team that shipped it as an MCP server from day one never had to think about this migration at all.
The plugin version cannot make that same claim, it was written for one host, and it stays written for one host until someone rebuilds it.
Multiply this by every tool a team owns, and the gap between the two approaches compounds fast.
15. Common Mistakes When Comparing the Two

items: Assuming any plugin like feature is automatically portable, portability comes from an open shared protocol, not from the word plugin itself.
Underestimating the rewrite cost of a second vendor specific plugin, it is usually a full rebuild, not a small tweak.
Treating MCP's upfront setup as wasted effort, it is the cost of reach across hosts that do not exist yet.
Forgetting that adoption depends on ease of implementation too, an open spec still has to be simple enough that vendors bother supporting it.
Assuming the earlier plugin era was pointless, it solved real problems and paved the way for lessons MCP later built on.

blocks.text: 16. Practice: Sketch Your Own Tool Both Ways
Take any tool idea, a lookup, a search, an action, and sketch it two ways, once as a plugin manifest for one specific product, once as an MCP tool function.

code.content:
my_tool_name = "..."
built_as_vendor_plugin = True   # tied to one AI product's format
built_as_mcp_server = True      # tied to no single vendor
# ask yourself: if a second AI product appears next year,
# which version reaches it without a rewrite?

blocks.text: Compare how much of the second version would need to change if a brand new AI assistant, one that does not exist yet, appeared next year and needed the same tool.
Write down the actual number of files or lines that would need touching in each version, the gap is usually bigger than expected.
Key Takeaway
Proprietary plugin systems tie a tool to one vendor's format, one review process, and one product's user base, so reaching a second product means rebuilding the whole thing.

MCP asks for a bit more upfront discipline in exchange for a server that keeps working across any compatible client, current or future, which is exactly why it spread across vendors in a way earlier plugin systems never did.
That tradeoff, a little more work now for a lot less rework later, is the whole argument in one sentence.
